clue.text: Title recollected by Beatles enthusiasts, primarily

definitions.text: Title recollected by Beatles enthusiasts, primarily

indicators.note: re-collected, gathered together again in a new order, so the letters of the first word are rearranged
primarily means taking the first letter of each of the two words just before it

explanation.surface: Fans of the Fab Four recall the name of one of their songs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'recollected' rearranges TITLE into LETIT; 'primarily' adds B and E, the initials of Beatles enthusiasts. The whole clue also describes the song title.
explanation.definitionFit: Let It Be is a famous Beatles song and album, exactly a title that their fans would recall.

clue.text: English type is in Paris a month? Not Jan!

parts.note: the French for 'is' is est

indicators.note: Not followed by a word means that word's letters are taken away from the month

parts.note: January is a month of the year
taken as written, the letters to be removed

explanation.surface: A puzzled query whether an English sort is found in Paris in some month other than January.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not Jan!' strips JAN from JANUARY, leaving UARY. Estuary English is the accent of London and the Thames estuary region.
explanation.definitionFit: Estuary English is a recognised variety of southern English speech, so it names an English type of accent.

clue.text: One close to London gets support coming up from the country

parts.note: one is I, the Roman numeral

indicators.note: the close of a word is its last letter, here of London
in a down answer, coming up means the word is read upwards, i.e. backwards

parts.note: aid is support or help

explanation.surface: Someone living near London finds backing rising from the nation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One close to London' reads like a commuter-belt resident; it is two separate pieces, a numeral and a final letter.
explanation.definitionFit: India is a nation in South Asia, so it is simply an example of a country.

clue.text: God help us if we listen

indicators.note: listening means we judge the words by their sound, not their spelling

parts.note: to back us is to help or support us

explanation.surface: A desperate plea for divine aid, if anyone up there is paying attention.
explanation.walkthrough: 'if we listen' says the phrase 'back us' is heard, giving the name of the god. 'God help us' looks like an exclamation of despair.
explanation.definitionFit: Bacchus is the Roman god of wine, the counterpart of the Greek Dionysus.

clue.text: Porridge put on a rack?

definitions.meaning: British slang for a prison sentence, as in the sitcom of that name; a stint inside is a term served
to extend a body on the torture rack is to pull it longer

explanation.walkthrough: Porridge is British slang for time served in prison; the oat breakfast is a decoy.
explanation.definitionFit: A stretch is a prison term in slang, and to stretch is what the rack does to its victim.

clue.text: Great weight on horse brought over from Polynesia

indicators.note: in a down answer, one piece on another sits above it

parts.note: a ton is a large unit of weight

indicators.note: brought over means turned round, so the word for horse is read backwards

parts.note: a nag is an old horse

explanation.surface: Something very heavy carried on horseback from the South Pacific.
explanation.walkthrough: 'brought over' reverses NAG to GAN, placed beneath TON.
explanation.definitionFit: Tongan describes someone or something from Tonga, an island kingdom in Polynesia.

clue.text: Thin person required to model 22 top

indicators.note: to model is to shape or mould, so the letters are reshaped

parts.note: the answer to clue 22 is used as letters here
taken as written

explanation.surface: A slim figure is wanted to show off a shiny garment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'model' shapes the nine letters of the 22-down answer plus TOP into a new word. 'model' looks like a catwalk job, fitting 'thin person'.
explanation.definitionFit: An ectomorph is a person with a lean, slight body type in the classic body-type scheme.

clue.text: Rich man endlessly annoyed about rising employment

indicators.note: about means going round the other piece
endlessly means the last letter is dropped

parts.note: cross means annoyed

indicators.note: in a down answer, rising means the word is read upwards, so reversed

parts.note: use is employment, as in putting to use

explanation.surface: A wealthy man, constantly irritated about his job prospects improving.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down answer 'rising' means read upwards; 'about' means the trimmed word wraps round the other piece.
explanation.definitionFit: Croesus was the fabulously wealthy king of Lydia, a byword for great riches.

clue.text: They say binder discloses what's said

parts.note: the word 'they', say, is an example of a pronoun
cement binds bricks together

explanation.surface: Rumour has it that a bookbinder reveals spoken words.
explanation.walkthrough: 'say' marks 'They' as an example of a part of speech; 'discloses' joins wordplay to definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A pronouncement is a formal declaration, something stated or said.

clue.text: A small earring makes a man sexually attractive

definitions.meaning: a small button-like earring fixed through the lobe
slang for a virile, attractive young man

explanation.surface: Wearing a tiny earring turns a man into a heartthrob.
explanation.definitionFit: A stud is both a small ear ornament and slang for a sexually attractive man.

clue.text: Innocent cook getting in a stew with a rich dish

indicators.note: in a stew means in a muddle, so the letters are jumbled

parts.note: taken as written, part of the letters to be mixed

explanation.surface: A naive chef gets flustered over a heavy meal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in a stew' mixes up INNOCENT COOK plus A RICH; 'stew' and 'cook' suggest the kitchen.
explanation.definitionFit: Coronation chicken is a cold dish of chicken in curried creamy sauce, created for the 1953 coronation.

clue.text: Conflict about a carriage

indicators.note: about means surrounding the other piece

parts.note: a clash is a conflict

explanation.surface: A dispute over a horse-drawn vehicle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' puts CLASH around A.
explanation.definitionFit: A calash is a light low-wheeled carriage with a folding hood.

clue.text: Local girl narrowly averted disaster

parts.note: near means local, close by
a miss is a girl or young woman

explanation.surface: A neighbourhood lass only just escaped catastrophe.
explanation.definitionFit: A near miss is an accident that only just failed to happen, a calamity barely avoided.

clue.text: Tossing my amusing work out here

indicators.note: tossing throws the letters about into a new order

explanation.surface: Someone throwing their funny essay away in disgust.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tossing' rearranges MY AMUSING. 'work out' looks like a noun for a piece of writing but is the verb for exercising.
explanation.definitionFit: A gymnasium is a place where people exercise, so it is where one works out.

clue.text: Resort hotel in Channel Islands — flipping ancient!

indicators.note: re-sort, to sort again, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: flipping means turned over, so the abbreviation is read backwards

parts.note: CI is the abbreviation for the Channel Islands, British isles off Normandy

explanation.surface: An exasperated tourist complaining that a holiday hotel in Jersey is terribly old.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Resort' rearranges HOTEL IN into NEOLITH; 'flipping' reverses CI to IC. 'Resort' and 'flipping' pose as a holiday spot and a mild oath.
explanation.definitionFit: Neolithic refers to the New Stone Age, so it means very ancient.

clue.text: Rank and number

definitions.meaning: rank as an adjective means flagrant or disgusting
a count of twelve dozen, i.e. 144

explanation.definitionFit: Gross means rank or coarse, and a gross is the number 144.

clue.text: Singer in a long-forgotten oratorio

indicators.note: in means the letters sit inside the words that follow

explanation.surface: A vocalist performs in an oratorio nobody remembers.
explanation.definitionFit: A tenor is a male singer with a high voice, a part often found in oratorios.

clue.text: English woods? Poppycock!

parts.note: yew is a kind of wood
ash is another kind of wood

explanation.surface: Someone dismissing English forests as nonsense.
explanation.walkthrough: 'woods' gives two trees, YEW and ASH, for its plural.
explanation.definitionFit: Eyewash is informal for nonsense or humbug, the same as poppycock.

clue.text: Something to eat and drink — everything extremely good

parts.note: Scotch is whisky, a drink

indicators.note: extremely takes the extreme letters, first and last, of the word before

explanation.surface: A party where the food and drink are all excellent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'extremely' takes E and G from 'everything'. A Scotch egg is a hard-boiled egg wrapped in sausage meat and breadcrumbs, a British picnic snack.
explanation.definitionFit: A Scotch egg is a savoury snack food, so it is something to eat.

clue.text: Bound to believe in 9?

indicators.note: the answer to clue 9 means something said, so the word is judged by how it is spoken

parts.note: to trust is to believe in

explanation.surface: Someone sure to have faith in a statement.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in 9?' means in pronunciation, so the word for believe in is heard as a word for tied up. 'Bound to' poses as 'certain to'.
explanation.definitionFit: Trussed means tied up tightly, as a chicken is before roasting, so bound.

clue.text: Ring for Madame found in rubbish

indicators.note: found in means the abbreviation sits inside the other word

parts.note: grot is British slang for rubbish or junk

explanation.surface: A ring belonging to a French lady turns up in the bin.
explanation.walkthrough: Grot is British slang for junk; 'found in' places the French title's abbreviation inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: A grommet is a ring or eyelet reinforcing a hole, so it is a type of ring.

clue.text: The Catholic church goes after church plate

indicators.note: goes after means the second piece follows the first

parts.note: Rome stands for the Roman Catholic Church

explanation.surface: The Church of Rome chasing another church for its silverware.
explanation.definitionFit: Chrome is chromium plating, a thin metal coating, so it means plate.

clue.text: One working with Morse, radio operator in part of London

parts.note: Lewis is the detective sergeant who works with Inspector Morse in the TV series
a ham is an amateur radio operator

explanation.surface: A telegraphist working in some district of the capital.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Morse' suggests Morse code and radio; it is Inspector Morse, the Oxford TV detective. Lewisham is a borough in south-east London.
explanation.definitionFit: Lewisham is a borough and district in south-east London.

clue.text: Turn back after relative almost gets clear

indicators.note: after means the turned piece comes second
almost means the last letter is left off

parts.note: an uncle is a relative

indicators.note: back means read backwards

parts.note: a go is a turn, as in a game

explanation.surface: Retreating after a family member nearly gets away.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turn back' looks like an instruction to retreat, but it is a noun for a go, written backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: To unclog is to clear a blockage from a pipe or drain.

clue.text: Desist from cold comfort

parts.note: C is the abbreviation for cold, as on taps
ease is comfort

explanation.surface: Stop seeking solace in the chill.
explanation.definitionFit: To cease is to stop, the same as to desist.

clue.text: A number of Romans refuse tips but they let you get ready

parts.note: C is the Roman numeral for 100
ash is refuse left after burning
points are tips, sharp ends

explanation.surface: Some Romans will not accept tips but are happy to help others prepare.
explanation.walkthrough: 'refuse' looks like a verb but is the noun, rubbish. 'ready' is cash, ready money.
explanation.definitionFit: Cash points are machines dispensing banknotes, i.e. ready money.

clue.text: A former railway charity

parts.note: LMS was the London, Midland and Scottish Railway, a British company before nationalisation

explanation.surface: An old railway turned into a charitable body.
explanation.definitionFit: Alms are gifts to the poor, so they are charity.

clue.text: See 11
Starved in order to get publicity

indicators.note: put in order means arranged anew, so the letters are reorganised

explanation.surface: Going hungry to get one's name noticed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in order' rearranges STARVED.
explanation.definitionFit: Adverts are advertisements, the material used for publicity.
